dick.et:
From Middle High German dicke, from Old High German dicki, dicchi (akin to Old Saxon thikki), from Proto-West Germanic *þikkwī.
Compare Low German dick, Dutch dik, English thick, Danish tyk.

s: seal, gasket (something designed to prevent liquids or gases from leaking through a joint)

Dicke.et: From Middle High German dicke, from Old High German dicchī; analysable as dick + -e.

In 2028 at the latest, they have to release something - otherwise this place is out of business.

Dickicht.et: Formed from dick (“thick”), similar to Old English þiccet.

Dickkopf.et: Bahuvrīhi compound of dick (“thick, big”) + Kopf (“head”). Attested 16th c. in the literal sense.

Dickbein.et: Formally from dick (“thick”) + Bein (“bone, leg”). Probably an alteration by popular etymology of *Diechbein, from obsolete Diech (“thigh”) + Bein. The former from Middle High German diech, from Old High German dioh, from Proto-Germanic *þeuhą.

s: Das ist ein dicker Hund, ich kann es nicht glauben.
That's a big deal, I can't believe it..
